name: Meridian Municipal Supply TearClear TC-4 'Dispersal'
description:
The TearClear TC-4 is Meridian Municipal Supply's standard-issue handheld tear gas canister, procured under the city's standing public safety equipment contract and distributed to all Meridian Municipal Security personnel as primary crowd-dispersal equipment. The TC-4 contains MMS-CS2, a standardized CS gas formulation with a stabilizing carrier that extends active suspension time to approximately four minutes in still air — longer in enclosed spaces. The design is deliberately utilitarian: a gray polymer-over-steel canister with a pull-ring safety, twist-lock actuator, and a wide-angle dispersal nozzle that creates a 90-degree forward cone. It is designed to be used with one hand, from behind a shield or barrier, and to function reliably after being dropped, soaked, or exposed to temperature extremes.

The TC-4 is not a sophisticated tool. It does not require training beyond a one-hour familiarization course. It does not require maintenance. It is purchased in bulk, distributed widely, and treated as expendable. Municipal supply contracts show recurring orders of several thousand units per quarter. The sheer ubiquity of the gray canister in Meridian's security landscape means it is as recognizable to Shelf residents as any police badge — and carries approximately the same emotional weight.

The TC-4 has been in continuous production and service since 2183 with only minor formulation updates. Its longevity is not a product of excellence but of institutional inertia, bulk contract pricing, and the absence of any political will to fund alternatives. It is the default answer to the question of how Meridian handles crowds it does not want.
legality: Licensed — standard issue to municipal security; licensed security firms may purchase with permit; civilian possession restricted
specifications:
Active compound: MMS-CS2 (CS gas, stabilized carrier)
Dispersal pattern: 90-degree forward cone
Effective area: approximately 12 square meters at 3m range
Active suspension time: 4 minutes (still air), longer in enclosed spaces
Onset: 15–30 seconds
Duration of effect: 15–30 minutes post-exposure
Canister: gray polymer-over-steel, pull-ring safety, twist-lock actuator
Weight: 0.31 kg
Dimensions: 18cm × 6cm
Price: Φ22 (municipal bulk contract); Φ65 (licensed security retail)
tactical_use: The TC-4 is deployed in standard crowd-dispersal formations — a line of security personnel each carrying one canister, deploying in sequence to create a moving wall of contaminated air that advances on a crowd. It is also used in building clearance and corridor denial, where the enclosed-space suspension extension makes it particularly effective. Operators are trained to deploy upwind and to target crowd depth rather than frontline individuals. The TC-4 is not a precision tool and is not intended as one — it is a bulk denial instrument for bulk situations.
cultural_context: The gray can is so thoroughly associated with municipal crackdowns that in some Shelf dialects 'getting gray-canned' simply means being subjected to any form of security force action. Children in Shelf districts learn to recognize the canister's profile before they learn to read. The TC-4's very mundanity is part of what makes it politically charged — it is not a military weapon, not exotic, not the product of some terrifying R&D program. It is a gray can bought in bulk, and that normalization of chemical crowd control is what activists point to when they argue that Meridian has institutionalized violence against its lowest tier.
story_hooks: A cache of several hundred TC-4 canisters has gone missing from a municipal supply depot — enough to gas an entire district, and someone apparently planned this in advance
